story: This Osage orange in Harlem has ended up in an art exhibition. Its twisting, wraparound trunk is referenced in Tree Reflections, a public art piece by Susan Stair that was shown at Conference House Park on Staten Island, a whole borough and a ferry ride away from the tree itself. That trunk is the reason to come. The local press coverage of the 2024 Great Trees list singled out its unique twisting form, and the Parks listing describes the trunk as wrapping around itself. It measures 58 inches across, about 4.6 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory gives exactly the same figure for the only Osage orange that size in the park. The inventory found it in Good condition in May 2026. NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in October 2024, when the city updated its roll of remarkable trees for the first time in about forty years. The description of the trunk reaches us through press coverage of the Parks listing, so treat it as second-hand. The measurement and the location come straight from the city's own inventory. It stands at the southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park, free public parkland in the middle of Harlem. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the twisting trunk that wraps around itself, 58 inches across. It stands at the southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park in Harlem.

story: When Mapes Park in the Bronx was rebuilt, the neighbours made sure this elm came through it. The press coverage of the 2024 Great Trees list says the tree inspired the neighbourhood to push for its preservation during the park renovations, and the Parks listing credits community members, working through the city's Community Parks Initiative, with protecting it. The park's ballfield was rebuilt under that same initiative in 2021. The tree the neighbours stood up for is worth the trip. Its trunk measures 62 inches across, about five metres round, which is large for an American elm growing in a city. It is also the only American elm of any real size in the park; the city's forestry inventory lists no other above 30 inches, and its 62 inch entry matches the Great Tree figure exactly. That inventory found it in Good condition in February 2026. NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in October 2024, putting a tree its neighbours had defended onto the city's roll of its most remarkable trees. The description reaches us through press coverage of the Parks listing, so treat the details as second-hand; the measurement and the location are the city's own. It stands in Mapes Park near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue, free public parkland. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 62 inches across, the one big American elm in the park. It stands in Mapes Park near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue in the Bronx.

story:
When New York's parks department revised its list of Great Trees in October 2024, the first revision in about forty years, Manhattan got exactly one new entry. It was this American sycamore in Morningside Park, standing beside a fork in the path just north of the West 120th Street entrance.

Its trunk is 48 inches across, about 3.8 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory rated it in good condition at its last inspection. It is also easy to overlook. New York is full of London planes, the hybrid that is the city's most common street tree, and this tree's parent species looks much like them at a glance. The plain American sycamore is the native one, the tree of eastern river valleys, and in Morningside it is the only one of its size.

The park itself is a long, steep strip of rock between Harlem below and Morningside Heights above, laid out in the late nineteenth century to deal with a cliff too sheer for streets. The sycamore grows in that park, with the Columbia campus a few blocks west on the heights and the subway a ten-minute walk away.

Nobody has published its height, its age or when it was planted, and the forestry record dates from 2017. If you know more, or have stood under it lately, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one native American sycamore among the London planes, its trunk about 3.8 metres round. It stands beside the path fork just north of the West 120th Street entrance.

story:
A fire in the 1970s left a gap on East 6th Street, and a weeping willow now taller than six storeys fills it. After the blaze the city cleared the burnt tenement and set the lot aside for community gardening. The Creative Little Garden opened in 1978 and has been run by volunteers ever since, and its willow, according to Village View's 2024 profile, spreads a canopy about 12 metres across over a blue stone patio.

In 2024 the parks department put the tree on its list of Great Trees, the first new additions in about forty years. Its measurements depend on who held the tape. The 2024 listing gives the trunk as 37 inches across. The city's forestry inventory, updated in July 2026, gives 42, about 3.35 metres round. The willow may simply have grown, or the two were measured at different heights.

By one account the willow was planted in 1978 as a community effort, the same year the garden opened. That date is reported rather than confirmed, so treat it as likely rather than settled. If you were there when it went in, tell us.

For a weeping willow in Manhattan, a tree that likes wet ground and open sky, to reach this size on a former tenement lot is the surprise. The garden opens at posted hours only, so check before going. Another big willow, in El Jardin del Paraiso, stands about 450 metres east, which makes a two-garden walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the weeping crown over the blue stone patio, more than six storeys high. It stands in the Creative Little Garden at 530 East 6th Street.

story:
When Tessa Huxley dug the hole for this tree in 1981, she scraped the top of the subway tunnel. The dawn redwood she planted in the Liz Christy Community Garden, at the Bowery and East Houston Street, now stands about 30 metres tall. You can pick it out along Houston Street from Avenue B all the way to Greene Street, a conifer rising over the low roofs, and it is noticeably cooler underneath.

The species has a stranger history than most. Dawn redwood was first described from fossils, and scientists assumed it was long extinct until living trees turned up in central China in the 1940s. Seed reached American gardens at the end of that decade. So a tree that the textbooks had buried grows here over a subway line, forty-five years after a volunteer put it in the ground.

That makes it young for a tree on New York's Great Trees list, which the parks department revised in 2024. It also makes its story unusually complete, down to the year, the gardener and what lay under the spade. For most old trees in this city, nobody wrote any of that down.

The garden is run by volunteers and opens only at posted hours, so check before going. The tree does not need the gate to be open. It is in view from Houston Street.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, a conifer about 30 metres tall standing over the low buildings, the only dawn redwood on the block. It stands inside the Liz Christy Community Garden at the Bowery and East Houston Street.

transport: Subway 1 to Van Cortlandt Park-242nd St, about 15 minutes' walk
story: This white ash has been cloned, and its copy grows elsewhere in the same park, at the south end of Van Cortlandt Park's Parade Ground. The original is the one worth the walk. It was on NYC Parks' first Great Trees list in 1985, and it is still alive in the years of the emerald ash borer, which has made a white ash this size a rare thing to find standing at all. The numbers have grown since that first list. In 1985 it measured 56.6 inches across the trunk and 82.8 feet tall. Parks now gives about 60 inches, nearly 4.8 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory, updated in May 2026, agrees on the 60 inches. That same record grades it Fair rather than Good, so this is a survivor, not an untouched one. It stands on the east side of the entrance to Van Cortlandt Park's cross-country trail, free public parkland in the Bronx. There is a second large ash within a hundred metres, at about 40 inches, so check the trunk; the big one is half as thick again. The Red Horse Chestnut of Van Cortlandt House is in the same park, which makes a two-tree walk. Two caveats on the sources. The 1985 figures come to us through a transcription of the Parks list, not the Parks page itself, and nobody has published an age. If you know it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 60 inches across, half as thick again as the 40 inch ash nearby. It stands on the east side of the entrance to the cross-country trail in Van Cortlandt Park.
